name: Epristeride
summary: A Chinese BPH drug of the finasteride family; hair-loss use was explored but never approved.
lead: Epristeride is an oral steroidal 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor that lowers conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT). It is marketed in China for benign prostatic hyperplasia under brand names including Aipuliete and Chuanliu .

name: Alfatradiol (Ell-Cranell Alpha)
summary: A weak topical estrogen sold in Germany for hair loss; seems to slow loss but regrows little.
lead: Alfatradiol, also called 17-alpha-estradiol, is a stereoisomer of the main human estrogen, 17-beta-estradiol. It is applied to the scalp as a low-concentration ethanolic solution to treat androgenetic alopecia in men and women, and is sold in Germany and several Latin American countries under names including Ell-Cranell Alpha, Pantostin, Avixis and Avicis .

name: Topilutamide (Fluridil)
summary: A topical antiandrogen sold in the Czech Republic and Slovakia for hair loss, with little published trial data.
lead: Topilutamide, also called fluridil (code BP-766), is a topical nonsteroidal antiandrogen applied to the scalp for pattern hair loss in men and women. It is marketed as a 2% product, Eucapil, by Interpharma Praha .

name: Dimethylcurcumin (ASC-J9)
summary: An experimental curcumin-derived anti-androgen that breaks down the androgen receptor; tried as an acne cream in two Phase 2 trials with no published results found.
lead: Dimethylcurcumin, known by the development code ASC-J9 (and also GO-Y025), is a synthetic curcumin derivative described as a nonsteroidal antiandrogen. Unlike conventional androgen receptor (AR) blockers, it is reported to work by promoting degradation of the androgen receptor protein rather than only occupying the receptor. It is listed as an experimental drug and is not approved for any use.

name: Drospirenone
summary: An antiandrogenic progestin in some contraceptive pills, FDA-labelled for moderate acne in women who also want birth control, with a debated clot-risk signal.
lead: Drospirenone is a synthetic progestin structurally related to the diuretic spironolactone. In addition to activating the progesterone receptor, it blocks the mineralocorticoid and androgen receptors, which gives it a profile that is often described as closer to natural progesterone than that of older progestins. It is taken by mouth, most often combined with an estrogen in contraceptive pills, and also as a progestogen-only pill.

name: Dienogest
summary: An antiandrogenic progestin used for endometriosis and in some pills that are prescribed for acne, with no acne-specific trials in the sources reviewed.
lead: Dienogest is a synthetic progestin derived from 19-nortestosterone, developed by Bayer's predecessor companies. It is used as a 2 mg standalone treatment for endometriosis in many countries and as the progestin in several combined oral contraceptives and menopausal products. It is sometimes called a fourth-generation progestin.

name: Chlormadinone acetate
summary: An antiandrogenic progestin in some European contraceptive pills used for acne and oily skin, supported by open-label data rather than large trials.
lead: Chlormadinone acetate (CMA) is a synthetic progestin derived from 17-hydroxyprogesterone. It has progestogenic activity together with antiandrogenic effects, acting both by blocking the androgen receptor and by lowering gonadotropin-driven hormone production. It is mostly used at 2 mg in combined oral contraceptives with ethinylestradiol (for example Belara), in some menopausal hormone therapies, and at higher doses for prostate conditions in Japan and South Korea.

name: Nomegestrol acetate
summary: A mildly antiandrogenic progestin in European pills; any acne benefit is suggested by its pharmacology, with no acne trial found.
lead: Nomegestrol acetate (NOMAC) is a synthetic progestin derived from 19-norprogesterone. It is a potent, selective progesterone receptor agonist that suppresses ovulation and has some antiandrogenic activity, with no important androgenic, estrogenic, glucocorticoid or antimineralocorticoid effects. It is used in combination with estradiol as a contraceptive pill (Zoely), for menopausal hormone therapy, and alone for certain gynaecological conditions (Lutenyl).

name: Abiraterone acetate
summary: A prescription prostate-cancer drug that blocks androgen synthesis; no hair or skin studies exist in the sources reviewed.
lead: Abiraterone acetate (brand names Zytiga and Yonsa) is an oral prodrug converted in the body to abiraterone, an inhibitor of the enzyme CYP17A1, which lowers production of androgens including testosterone and DHT. It is approved for advanced prostate cancer, given with prednisone, and is a prescription cancer drug rather than a cosmetic or dermatological product.

name: Cimetidine
summary: An acid-reducing H2 blocker with weak antiandrogen action that has been floated for acne and hirsutism; references describe the effect as too weak to matter.
lead: Cimetidine (brand name Tagamet) is a histamine H2-receptor antagonist that reduces stomach acid, used mainly for ulcers and heartburn.  It also has weak antiandrogenic activity, which is why it has occasionally been tried for acne and excess hair growth (hirsutism) in women.

name: Erythromycin (acne)
summary: A prescription macrolide antibiotic solution for acne, usually paired with benzoyl peroxide because acne bacteria can become resistant.
lead: Erythromycin is a macrolide antibiotic that blocks bacterial protein synthesis.  A 2% topical solution is labelled in the US for the treatment of acne vulgaris.

name: Sulfacetamide
summary: An old sulfa antibiotic, usually paired with sulfur in prescription lotions and washes for acne, rosacea and seborrheic dermatitis.
lead: Sulfacetamide is a sulfonamide antibiotic used on the eyes and skin.  In dermatology it is most often sold as sodium sulfacetamide, frequently combined with sulfur, for acne vulgaris, rosacea with papules and pustules, and seborrheic dermatitis.

name: Nadifloxacin
summary: A topical quinolone antibiotic cream for acne used in Japan, parts of Europe and Asia but not the US.
lead: Nadifloxacin is a topical fluoroquinolone antibiotic used mainly for acne vulgaris and, secondarily, for bacterial skin infections.  It inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase.

name: Azithromycin pulse (acne)
summary: Short intermittent courses of an oral macrolide antibiotic used off-label for inflammatory acne; evidence is small head-to-head trials and resistance is a stated concern.
lead: Azithromycin pulse dosing for acne refers to the use of the oral macrolide antibiotic azithromycin in short, intermittent courses (for example on a few days each week) as a treatment for inflammatory acne vulgaris. It is an off-label dermatology practice in many countries; azithromycin is a prescription-only antibiotic, and the pulse schedule is a prescriber's decision rather than a product category.

name: Aminolevulinic acid photodynamic therapy
summary: A clinic procedure pairing topical ALA with light to treat actinic keratoses; its acne use is investigational, with mixed trial signals.
lead: Aminolevulinic acid photodynamic therapy (ALA PDT) is a procedure in which aminolevulinic acid, a precursor of heme, is applied to the skin and the area is then illuminated with a specific light source. The skin converts ALA into protoporphyrin IX, a light-sensitive compound that produces reactive oxygen species when illuminated and damages targeted cells.

name: Trichloroacetic acid (TCA peel)
summary: A medium-depth chemical peel acid used by clinicians for skin texture, pigment and scars; registered trials exist but outcomes aren't reported in the records.
lead: Trichloroacetic acid (TCA) is a strong organic acid used in dermatology as a chemical peel and as a topical agent to destroy warts. It was discovered by the French chemist Jean-Baptiste Dumas in 1839, and in laboratories is widely used to precipitate proteins and nucleic acids.

name: Corticosteroid injection (Kenalog for cysts)
summary: A clinician-injected steroid (triamcinolone) used off-label on single inflamed pimples; no acne-cyst trials were found in the sources used.
lead: Intralesional corticosteroid injection means injecting a small amount of a corticosteroid, most often triamcinolone acetonide (brand name Kenalog), directly into a skin lesion such as an inflamed acne nodule or cyst. Acne forums describe it as a way to reduce the size and redness of an individual pimple, and it is a clinician-administered procedure.

name: Basil oil (acne)
summary: A plant essential oil with lab antibacterial activity, including against the acne bacterium in vitro; no human acne studies were found.
lead: Basil oil is an essential oil steam-distilled from basil (Ocimum basilicum). European basil oil is high in linalool and methyl chavicol (estragole), roughly 3:1, with smaller amounts of 1,8-cineole, eugenol and myrcene; composition varies with cultivar.

name: Seaweed oligosaccharides
summary: Brown-seaweed-derived sugars marketed as a complementary topical acne ingredient; support is one literature review.
lead: Seaweed oligosaccharides are short carbohydrate chains derived from the polysaccharide cell wall of brown seaweed, notably Laminaria digitata (oarweed), studied as a topical, marine-derived ingredient for acne. A published review also describes a seaweed oligosaccharide-zinc complex (SOZC).

name: Bumetanide
summary: A potent prescription loop diuretic that appears in gray-market "water pill" talk; no study has tested it for facial puffiness.
lead: Bumetanide is a loop diuretic, a prescription medicine that increases the amount of sodium and water the kidneys excrete. It is sold as Bumex, Burinex and, in a nasal-spray form, Enbumyst, among other names, and is used to treat edema (fluid retention) associated with heart failure, liver disease and kidney disease.

name: Torsemide
summary: A prescription loop diuretic for heart-failure fluid overload; mentioned in depuffing circles but never studied for appearance.
lead: Torsemide, also spelled torasemide, is a loop diuretic and sulfonamide used mainly to relieve fluid accumulation from heart failure, kidney disease and liver disease. It can be given orally or intravenously and is sold under names such as Demadex.

name: Hydrochlorothiazide
summary: A common prescription thiazide diuretic for blood pressure; some forum users discuss it as a daily water pill, but it has not been studied for appearance.
lead: Hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ) is a thiazide diuretic used to treat high blood pressure, edema from heart failure and other conditions, and sometimes to reduce kidney stone recurrence. It became commercially available in 1959, is on the WHO Essential Medicines List, and was the 18th most prescribed drug in the US in 2024, according to Wikipedia.
claims: HCTZ is a safer, better alternative to furosemide for water retention.

name: Chlortalidone
summary: A long-acting thiazide-like blood-pressure diuretic; a possible water pill in forum lists, with no appearance data.
lead: Chlortalidone (chlorthalidone) is an oral thiazide-like diuretic used as a first-line treatment for hypertension and for edema from heart, liver or kidney disease. It is also used for nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, renal tubular acidosis and preventing calcium kidney stones.

name: Indapamide
summary: A thiazide-like blood-pressure diuretic with big stroke-prevention trials behind it, but nothing on appearance or depuffing.
lead: Indapamide is a thiazide-like diuretic used mainly for hypertension and for edema from congestive heart failure. It was patented in 1968, approved for medical use in 1977, and appears on the WHO Essential Medicines List.

name: Metolazone
summary: A potent thiazide-like diuretic mostly used alongside loop diuretics in heart failure; no appearance data exists.
lead: Metolazone is a thiazide-like diuretic sold as Zaroxolyn, Zytanix, Mykrox and Metoz. It was patented in 1966 and approved for medical use in 1974. It treats edema from heart failure, kidney disease and cirrhosis and is used for hypertension, though hydrochlorothiazide is more commonly used for blood pressure.

name: Acetazolamide (Diamox)
summary: A sulfonamide carbonic anhydrase inhibitor used for glaucoma, edema and altitude sickness; it is a diuretic, but nothing shows it reduces facial puffiness.
lead: Acetazolamide, sold under the brand name Diamox among others, is a sulfonamide-derived carbonic anhydrase inhibitor that increases the kidney's excretion of bicarbonate, sodium and water. It is an older prescription drug used for glaucoma, certain edemas, some seizure disorders and the prevention of acute mountain sickness.

name: Triamterene
summary: A potassium-sparing diuretic for edema and hypertension; no study has tested it for facial puffiness, and its label warns of fatal hyperkalemia.
lead: Triamterene is a potassium-sparing diuretic that blocks epithelial sodium channels in the late distal tubule and collecting duct of the kidney, increasing sodium and water excretion while limiting potassium loss. It is used for edema and hypertension, most often in a fixed combination with hydrochlorothiazide.

name: Amiloride
summary: A mild potassium-sparing diuretic used with other diuretics; no research addresses facial puffiness, and hyperkalemia carries a boxed warning.
lead: Amiloride is a potassium-sparing diuretic that directly blocks epithelial sodium channels (ENaC) in the distal nephron, producing a mild increase in sodium and water excretion while conserving potassium. It is used mainly alongside thiazide or other potassium-wasting diuretics in heart failure and hypertension.

name: Eplerenone
summary: A selective aldosterone blocker for heart failure and hypertension, discussed on forums mainly as a pricey spironolactone alternative; no appearance studies exist.
lead: Eplerenone (brand name Inspra) is a selective aldosterone receptor antagonist and potassium-sparing diuretic. The US label lists two indications: improving survival in stable adults with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction after a myocardial infarction, and treating hypertension.
claims: Eplerenone is a pricey alternative to other options for people who want an aldosterone blocker.

name: Tolvaptan
summary: A prescription vasopressin blocker that makes the body excrete free water; it is approved for hyponatremia and kidney disease, with a boxed liver-injury warning and no appearance data.
lead: Tolvaptan is a selective vasopressin V2-receptor antagonist that causes aquaresis, the excretion of free water without major loss of electrolytes. It is used to treat clinically significant hyponatremia (brand Samsca) and to slow kidney function decline in adults at risk of rapidly progressing autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (brand Jynarque).
